what: Binary migration's primary goal per user is SOURCE CODE PROTECTION, not distribution simplicity or hook consolidation. npm's model exposed source; user wants closed-source distribution. Plan §1 lists three goals as co-equal — user clarified source protection is the one that matters. Implication: if Bun compile hits blockers (better-sqlite3, signing, size), alternatives optimized for source protection are in scope — bytenode (V8 bytecode via normal npm, ~1 day, medium-high protection), obfuscated minified npm (~2 hours, low-med protection), Node SEA / pkg / nexe (similar to Bun), full Rust/Go rewrite (weeks, strong). None of the JS-to-binary approaches (Bun, SEA, pkg, bytenode) stop a determined reverse-engineer — all produce extractable artifacts; they stop casual inspection. Strong protection requires compiled native code (Rust/Go).
why: User explicitly clarified this turn. The plan treats three goals as equal, but the user treats source protection as the driver. Future phase spawns need this to make correct tradeoffs — if Phase N hits a Bun-specific blocker, the question "is the cost worth it?" depends on whether source protection is THE goal (cheaper alternatives exist) or part of a bundle with distribution + hook consolidation (then Bun is the right all-in-one answer).
